case_study_insert.main_stem: Zenith Nut and Coupling (ZNC) is a workers' cooperative in the industrial fastener sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2007 by Ravi Zenith, it supplies stainless couplings to marine-engine builders and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. ZNC plans to invest $800,000 in a new thread-rolling machine, financed by $200,000 of member share capital, a $400,000 bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $270,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.20 a unit and a selling price of $13.20, and produces 90,000 units a year. ZNC faces a defect rate of 2.9% on rolled threads and rising labour turnover among machinists at its harbour-side works.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research and Operations Summary — Q1 2025: The thread-rolling line produced 22,500 couplings with a defect rate of 2.9%, down from 3.8% a year earlier. Rejected batches rose from 9 to 16 a month, and delivery time averaged 5.8 days. A survey of 300 marine-engine builders found 63% rank corrosion resistance first and 49% would pay a premium for certified stainless couplings. Staff records show 8 of 50 machinists left in the last six months; a certification course costs $720 per person.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Zenith Nut and Coupling as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (May 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.50%, increasing borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.5% from $12.70 to $13.65 per hour from April 2026. (3) Wholesale stainless-steel prices have risen 9.4% year-on-year, while engineering input inflation is 6.0% and marine-engine orders are forecast to grow 2.2%.

questions.question_text: ZNC is financing its $800,000 thread-rolling machine with $200,000 of member share capital, a $400,000 bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for ZNC of using member share capital instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Member share capital does not require interest or fixed repayments, so ZNC can keep its $400,000 loan for working capital while meeting $270,000 of fixed costs. The $200,000 raised from members can fund training at $720 per person to cut the 2.9% defect rate, without adding to the debt burden that would be expensive at the higher base rate.

Point 2: Share capital from members reinforces the cooperative's democratic ownership and keeps decision-making with the 50 workers rather than a lender. With 8 of 50 machinists having left in six months, member commitment helps stabilise the workforce, and the $800,000 machine can be installed without new collateral. A bank loan would impose covenants and interest that could strain cash if marine orders grow only 2.2%. Member capital also signals commitment to Ravi Zenith's cooperative, which helps when recruiting machinists after 8 of 50 left, whereas added borrowing would have to be serviced from the $6.00 contribution per unit.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to ZNC.

questions.question_text: ZNC is seeking marine-engine contracts. Consider a marine trade exhibition, a search-engine advertising campaign, or a direct sales team. Which should ZNC choose to win business? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Marine trade exhibition: A stand lets ZNC show certified stainless couplings and discuss corrosion resistance with engine builders face to face, which suits the 63% who rank it first. Exhibitions gather many buyers in one place. Costs stand fees, travel and staff time, however, and with a workforce of 50 and 8 of 50 machinists already having left, pulling people away from the 22,500-coupling line could worsen the 5.8-day delivery time.

Search-engine advertising: Paid ads reach builders actively looking for couplings and can be measured by clicks and enquiries. It is cheaper than a stand and can target marine-engine terms precisely. The drawback is that clicks are not contracts; the 49% who would pay a premium for certification need proof, and an ad cannot answer technical questions or reassure buyers about the 16 rejected batches a month as well as a person can.

Direct sales team: A sales engineer can visit marine-engine builders, present corrosion-test data and agree delivery dates. This directly addresses the 63% who put corrosion resistance first and the 49% seeking certified couplings, while allowing ZNC to explain how it will cut rejected batches. The cost is salaries and travel, and one small team cannot cover every port.

Recommendation: ZNC should choose a direct sales team. Certified technical selling converts the 63% and 49% identified in the survey and lets the cooperative defend the premium price, which neither a passive stand nor search ads can match consistently. The exhibition is rejected because of its cost and the strain on 50 staff; search advertising is rejected because it generates enquiries rather than the technical trust marine buyers require. ZNC should support the team with a simple website.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Lists the three marketing routes with little application to ZNC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Compares at least two routes using ZNC's survey and staffing data with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three routes in ZNC's context, recommends a sales team and explains why exhibitions and ads are rejected.

questions.question_text: ZNC's defect rate is 2.9% and 8 of 50 machinists left in six months. Explain two benefits for ZNC of democratic leadership in reducing labour turnover.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership lets the 50 worker-membersvote on shift patterns and quality targets, giving machinists a genuine say in how the $800,000 thread-rolling machine is run. Involvement raises job satisfaction and addresses the labour turnover shown by 8 of 50 leavers, retaining the skills needed to cut the 2.9% defect rate.

Point 2: Consultation gathers practical ideas from the machinists closest to the rolled threads, so problems behind 16 rejected batches a month can be solved faster. In a cooperative, participation also strengthens commitment to the $200,000 of member capital and the $400,000 loan, protecting the $13.20 selling price and the 49% of buyers who will pay a premium for certified couplings. With 22,500 couplings produced each quarter, a suggestion from a machinist can be tested quickly, so the 16 rejected batches a month can fall and the premium can be earned through direct sales and protect the $13.20 selling price.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to ZNC.

questions.question_text: ZNC wants to cut its 2.9% defect rate. Consider the $720 external certification course or on-the-job mentoring by experienced machinists. Which should ZNC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
External certification course: At $720 per person, a recognised qualification teaches up-to-date threading techniques and gives customers proof of competence, which matters to the 49% who would pay a premium for certified couplings. It can raise quality across the 22,500 couplings made each quarter. The cost is significant for a cooperative with $270,000 fixed costs, and sending machinists off the line while 8 of 50 have already left could lengthen the 5.8-day delivery time.

On-the-job mentoring: Experienced machinists train colleagues on the actual thread-rolling machine, so guidance matches ZNC's settings and helps reduce the 2.9% defect rate and 16 monthly rejected batches immediately. No course fee is paid and no worker leaves the harbour-side works, which protects output and eases the pressure that caused 8 of 50 to leave. Mentoring depends on the patience and skill of the mentors and provides no external certificate, so it may not satisfy buyers who want formal proof.

Decision: ZNC should choose on-the-job mentoring first. It attacks the 2.9% defect rate on the exact machine, avoids the $720 fee for every worker and keeps all 50 members at work while deliveries average 5.8 days. The external course is rejected for now because it removes staff and costs cash when 8 of 50 have already left; ZNC should certify a few mentors later to satisfy the 49% seeking certified suppliers. With 22,500 couplings made each quarter and 16 rejected batches a month, quick feedback on the actual machine is worth more than a generic qualification in the short term, and it keeps all 50 worker-members at the harbour-side works.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training options with little application to ZNC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the costs and benefits of one or both options using ZNC's defect, delivery and staff data.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates both options in context, recommends mentoring and clearly rejects full external certification.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how ZNC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $270,000 ÷ ($13.20 − $7.20) = $270,000 ÷ $6.00 = 45,000 units. | Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $13.20 − $7.20 = $6.00. | (iii) Four contextual uses explained.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $270,000 ÷ ($13.20 − $7.20) = $270,000 ÷ $6.00 = 45,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 45,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $13.20 − $7.20 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways ZNC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Break-even of 45,000 units against 90,000 produced gives a margin of safety of 45,000 units, showing how much output could fall before a loss.
2. Contribution of $6.00 lets managers assess the 49% premium opportunity: a $0.30 surcharge raises contribution to $6.30, cutting break-even to 42,857 units.
3. Break-even of 45,000 units indicates the sales needed before the $400,000 loan and $200,000 member capital can be rewarded, guiding production targets.
4. Unit cost of $270,000 ÷ 90,000 + $7.20 = $10.20 can be tracked against the 2.9% defect rate to judge whether the $800,000 machine is reducing waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate ZNC's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has ZNC's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.38 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.50 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.88 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.89 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $100,000 inventories + $125,000 trade receivables + $50,000 cash = $275,000; 2025 current assets = $115,000 + $140,000 + $30,000 = $285,000. The broader liquidity measure is $275,000 ÷ $200,000 = 1.375, about 1.38, in 2024 and $285,000 ÷ $190,000 = 1.50 in 2025. Excluding inventories, the stricter measure is ($275,000 − $100,000) ÷ $200,000 = $175,000 ÷ $200,000 = 0.875, about 0.88, in 2024 and ($285,000 − $115,000) ÷ $190,000 = $170,000 ÷ $190,000 = 0.89 in 2025.

Evaluation: The headline picture looks better but the improvement is weak. The broader measure rose from 1.38 to 1.50 mainly because current liabilities fell from $200,000 to $190,000, while current assets grew only $10,000. The stricter measure barely moved, from 0.88 to 0.89, and remains below 1.0, so ZNC still depends on selling inventories to meet short-term obligations. Cash actually fell from $50,000 to $30,000, which is concerning while the cooperative services a $400,000 loan and commits $800,000 to a new machine. Inventories rose to $115,000 despite a 2.9% defect rate and 16 rejected batches a month, so some stock may be slow to sell, and receivables climbed to $140,000.

Conclusion: ZNC's liquidity has not meaningfully improved. The broader measure is higher, but the stricter measure at 0.89 and the fall in cash show the gain relies on inventory rather than liquid funds. Management should rebuild cash and tighten credit control before expanding further.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States isolated financial figures or vague comments about liquidity with no accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both years with some contextual comment on the trend for ZNC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables, cash and current liabilities, and a justified conclusion on whether ZNC's liquidity improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for ZNC of offering a certified corrosion-resistance test with its stainless couplings.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey found 63% of marine-engine builders rank corrosion resistance first and 49% would pay a premium for certified couplings, so a test certificate supports the $13.20 price and helps justify the $800,000 thread-rolling investment. It also counters the 2.9% defect rate by proving quality to buyers.

Disadvantage: Testing and paperwork add time to the 5.8-day delivery and cost money when 8 of 50 machinists have left and a certification course is $720 per person. A failed test would expose the 16 rejected batches a month to customers, and the cooperative must fund the $400,000 loan from the $6.00 contribution per unit, so extra quality costs cannot easily be absorbed. Certification also gives the sales team evidence for the 63% of builders who rank corrosion resistance first, supporting the $13.20 price and helping recover the $800,000 investment. The cooperative must weigh that against the $400,000 loan and 8 of 50 leavers: testing adds duties to a short-staffed workshop, and any failed batch publicises the 16 rejected batches a month.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to ZNC.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.50%, the 7.5% minimum wage increase and the 9.4% rise in stainless-steel prices will affect ZNC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.50%): The rise is 0.75 percentage points. If the $400,000 bank loan is variable-rate, extra interest is 0.75% × $400,000 = $3,000 a year (0.0075 × $400,000), manageable against $270,000 fixed costs but a drain on funds for the $800,000 machine. If the loan is fixed, the direct effect is deferred.

Minimum wage increase (7.5%, from $12.70 to $13.65): Each hour rises by $13.65 − $12.70 = $0.95. ZNC has a workforce of 50 but the insert gives no hours worked, so no annual total may be assumed. Productivity is 90,000 units ÷ 50 = 1,800 units per worker; if that is maintained, the $13.20 price can absorb the rise. With 8 of 50 machinists having left and $720 certification costs, any fall in productivity would quickly raise unit labour cost.

Stainless-steel inflation (9.4%): The insert does not split the $7.20 variable cost, so an explicit bound is the honest method: if all of it were steel-linked, 9.4% × $7.20 = $0.6768, about $0.68 a unit; over 90,000 units that is roughly $60,912 a year. Even one sixth of that, about $10,000, exceeds the loan interest increase and would cut the $6.00 contribution while the 2.9% defect rate already wastes material.

Conclusion: The 9.4% rise in stainless-steel prices will have the greatest impact. It touches every coupling, cannot be removed by fixing a loan rate and directly erodes the contribution needed for the $800,000 investment. The interest rise is small and conditional; the wage rise is absorbable while productivity holds near 1,800 units per worker.
